implementation_notes: Swift has no synchronized keyword, so structural release comes from withLock on a lock type: os.OSAllocatedUnfairLock (iOS 16 / macOS 13 and later) owns its protected state and runs the closure under the lock, and the Swift 6 Synchronization module's Mutex offers the same closure API, so the critical section is the closure and release is guaranteed on every path, including thrown errors. NSLock.withLock provides the shape for older deployments. The manual os_unfair_lock_lock/unlock pair is justified only where those APIs are unavailable, since there the unlock can once again be forgotten.
pitfalls: The closure must not call back into the same lock (no reentrancy) and must not suspend or perform long work: an unfair lock held across a lock hop or I/O stalls other threads.
OSAllocatedUnfairLock and NSLock.withLock need iOS 16 / macOS 13; older deployment targets fall back to manual os_unfair_lock, where a forgotten unlock is possible again.
A scoped lock protects synchronous access only; state also touched from async code cannot await inside the closure, so such state belongs in an actor.

variants.name: actor isolation (compiler-serialized state)
variants.idiom_name: actor with isolated state, accessed with await
variants.implementation_notes: The Swift-native form of the pattern: an actor's mutable state is reachable only through its isolated methods and the runtime serializes those calls, so mutual exclusion is a property of the type rather than a lock call - there is nothing to acquire and nothing to forget. It is the default for shared mutable state in Swift concurrency; scoped withLock guards remain appropriate for synchronous hot paths where an await hop is unacceptable, and an explicit lock is still justified inside a non-isolated synchronous API that must not become async.
pitfalls: Actor reentrancy: an await inside an isolated method suspends and lets other tasks enter, so isolation is not a critical section across awaits - re-check invariants after every suspension.
Actor hops cost context switches, so putting hot synchronous state behind an actor can be slower than an unfair lock.
Isolation is per instance: global mutable state, statics and @unchecked Sendable types are outside actor protection.
